sections.title: Air vibration and acoustic phonetics
teaching: **Acoustic phonetics studies the sound produced by speech**, including vibration of the air in the vocal tract. The air is a moving physical medium, not simply empty space between the tongue and the palate.
Changes in tract shape alter how that air can vibrate. The resulting acoustic pattern carries information about the speech movements that shaped the passage.

sections.title: Why scientific understanding of AI matters
teaching: **Understanding AI requires examining how it works and what its behavior supports**. Social consequences and useful applications both make its mechanisms worth studying carefully.

A convincing response is an observation about behavior, while a theory of how it was produced is a separate explanation. Examining inputs, learned representations and outputs helps connect the behavior to a testable account.

sections.title: Course goals
Moving from memorization to creative reasoning
teaching: **Understanding involves explaining relationships and applying ideas**, rather than remembering isolated phrases. Two things that look different can share a mechanism, while similar-looking outcomes can have different causes.
A useful comparison identifies which relationships stay the same and which details change. Asking a new question about a familiar example can reveal whether the underlying explanation is understood.

sections.title: Voicing and place through sustained fricatives
teaching: **Fricatives keep air flowing through a narrow constriction**, producing turbulent sound. Their place of articulation identifies where the narrowing occurs, and voicing identifies whether the vocal folds vibrate.
The sounds /f/ and /v/ share a lip-and-teeth constriction but differ in voicing. The sounds /s/ and /z/ share an alveolar constriction and form the same voiceless–voiced contrast.

sections.title: Stop place, voicing, and nasality
teaching: **Stops involve a complete oral closure**, but the route available to the air determines whether the sound is oral or nasal. The tongue or lips can close the mouth while a lowered velum leaves a path through the nose.

sections.title: AI as a model of psychological abilities
teaching: **AI models abilities such as recognizing, attending, acting and learning** through numerical computation. These abilities are related but should not be treated as one undifferentiated operation.

Recognition uses current representations to identify an input, while learning changes those representations after experience. An account of knowing must connect what the system has learned to the decisions it can make.

sections.title: Taylor’s cloze procedure
teaching: **Closure is the completion of an incomplete pattern**, such as perceiving a triangle when its edges are not fully drawn. The perceived whole depends on organization supplied beyond the individual marks.

A cloze task removes part of a sequence and asks for a suitable completion. Completing it well requires using relationships among the available parts rather than responding to each part independently.

sections.title: What successful completion requires
teaching: **A completion task probes knowledge by asking what fits the available context**. Predicting the missing part of a sequence requires information about how its elements usually relate.
A language model represents the context numerically and computes a distribution over possible continuations. The learned weights determine which completions receive more support.

sections.title: From words to vectors and next-word probabilities
teaching: **Next-item prediction applies to a sequence of numerical vectors**, regardless of what those vectors represent. Words, sound, images and other data can all be represented as numbers for a model to process.
The model uses the available context to assign probabilities to possible continuations. Learning improves those probabilities when the actual continuation supplies feedback.

sections.title: Weights carry the system’s learned knowledge
teaching: **Learned weights carry information used to turn an input into a prediction**. Their collective values determine which relationships between the supplied signal and possible answers the model has learned.
The input describes the present case, while the parameters supply a learned way of processing it. Training changes those parameters using feedback about the model’s mistakes.

sections.title: Weights and synapses as a scale comparison
teaching: **Knowledge can be distributed across a very large set of connections**. A model’s many weights and the brain’s many synaptic connections motivate a comparison about distributed organization.

The comparison answers the objection that a large number of learned values is automatically unlike biological knowledge. It directs attention to how connections jointly support useful behavior rather than to one isolated stored fact.

sections.title: Mistakes provide a direction for learning

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
A staged shortest-path problem
teaching: **A state value summarizes the best remaining cost from that state to the goal**. It represents an entire optimal continuation rather than just the cost of one outgoing edge.
For each available next state, add the edge cost to that next state’s solved value. Choose the smallest resulting total to obtain the value for the current state.

sections.title: Why the locally cheapest choice can lose
teaching: **A greedy route algorithm chooses the cheapest available next step** without evaluating all later consequences. The first inexpensive edge can lead into an expensive remainder of the route.
The cost of a complete path is the sum of its successive edges. A locally favorable choice therefore does not establish that the total route is cheapest.

sections.title: Blank source page
Exhaustive search trades speed for certainty
teaching: **Exhaustive search evaluates every possible complete path** and compares their total costs. It can identify the best route in the supplied finite problem because no candidate path is omitted.
Many complete routes contain overlapping pieces, so evaluating each independently repeats work. The number of candidates can grow rapidly as the problem becomes larger.

sections.title: Bellman’s decomposition
teaching: **Dynamic programming solves shared subproblems once and reuses their answers**. A large problem can be built from smaller problems whose solutions are needed by several alternatives.

In a shortest-path problem, the cheapest remaining cost from a state can be calculated from the costs of its outgoing edges and the already solved destination states. Reusing those values prevents each complete route from recalculating the same remainder.

teaching: **Vowels differ in the shape of the vocal tract**, including where the tongue narrows the passage and whether the lips are rounded. These changes alter the resonances of the air without requiring a new vibrating source for each vowel.

A high front tongue position produces the vowel in dean, while a high back position with rounded lips produces the vowel in dune. A lower tongue configuration produces a more open vowel such as the one represented by /a/.

Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target
teaching: **A probability distribution has no negative entries and sums to one**. Its entries describe how the network allocates probability across the available categories.

The position of an entry determines which category it refers to. A target for dean puts one at the dean position and zero at the other positions, giving the training process a specific desired answer.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error
teaching: **A proposed weight change must be traced through the sign of the incoming activation and the desired output**. For a positive incoming activation, increasing a direct output weight raises that output’s raw score.

If that category is already receiving too much probability, pushing its score upward works against the target. For an early hidden weight, the overall effect also depends on downstream weights and pathways.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations
teaching: **Backpropagation starts at the output because the error is most directly connected to the last processing layer**. An early weight affects the result through several intermediate layers, so its contribution is harder to work out directly.

The algorithm computes downstream error information first and reuses it to determine the effects of earlier weights. This is the dynamic-programming idea of solving smaller dependent problems before the larger problems that contain them.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row
teaching: **Each input row must stay paired with its correct target row**. The input row contains the recording’s F1 and F2, while the target row identifies its vowel among the five output categories.
For dean, the target has a one in the dean column and zeros elsewhere. Moving an input row without its target would teach the network the wrong association even if every number remained well formed.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch
teaching: **The training code separates making a prediction, calculating loss, calculating gradients and updating weights**. Importing PyTorch supplies existing tools for these operations rather than requiring each algorithm to be written again.

The loss compares the prediction with the targets, and loss.backward() calculates gradients through the network. The optimizer’s step then updates the parameters using those gradients and the chosen learning rate.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation
teaching: **Sigmoid converts a neuron’s weighted sum into a bounded activation between zero and one**. Large negative sums produce values near zero, large positive sums produce values near one, and a sum of zero produces one half.
The S-shaped curve is steepest near the middle and flatter near the extremes. Similar changes in the input can therefore have different effects depending on where they fall on the curve.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity
teaching: **A changed hidden activation changes the inputs received by later layers**. Applying sigmoid therefore requires recomputing the downstream network rather than replacing one number and leaving the final decision untouched.
Each hidden neuron first combines its weighted inputs and then applies the nonlinear function. The transformed value is what travels through the outgoing connections.

sections.title: NNs → LLMs → Agentic Systems
Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories
teaching: **A mathematical neuron models a relationship between incoming activity, connection strengths and an output**. It simplifies biological processing into operations that can be calculated and studied.

The weights correspond to the different influences assigned to incoming signals. A weighted sum expresses one aspect of integration without reproducing every chemical and electrical detail of a biological neuron.

sections.title: Jordan’s recurrent network for speech production
teaching: **A recurrent network carries information from one step into another**, allowing its current processing to depend on prior state. This extends a network that classifies one static vector at a time.
Feedback supplies context for the next computation, making a sequence more than a collection of independent inputs. Speech production and prediction both depend on information unfolding through time.

sections.title: From one neuron to agentic systems
teaching: **A neuron, a network, a sequence model and an agentic system describe different levels of organization**. A neuron combines inputs, a network combines processing stages, and a sequence model uses context to predict a continuation.
An agentic system connects models through messages and assigned tasks. Its graph of interactions sits outside the hidden processing layers of an individual model.

sections.title: Fifteen vectors · the same next-item question for any sequence
teaching: **Next-item prediction applies to a sequence of numerical vectors**, regardless of what those vectors represent. Words, sound, images and other data can all be represented as numbers for a model to process.
The model uses the available context to assign probabilities to possible continuations. Learning improves those probabilities when the actual continuation supplies feedback.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?
teaching: **Phonotactics concerns which sound sequences a language allows**. English permits some consonant combinations before or after a vowel while excluding others in the same position.
An onset occurs before a syllable’s vowel, and a coda occurs after it. A cluster that works across a syllable boundary does not necessarily work at the beginning of a syllable.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge
teaching: **A next-letter choice can reveal knowledge of allowed word patterns**. After sp at the beginning of a word, a vowel, l or r fits familiar English patterns, while n does not fit the onset pattern used here.

Some beginnings permit many continuations while others sharply restrict the possibilities. A probability distribution can express that difference by spreading probability broadly or concentrating it on fewer choices.
